## Teaching Philosophy {#philosophy}

::: {.philosophy}
::: {.philo-verse lang="ar" dir="rtl"}
[إِذِ الْفَتَى حَسْبَ اعْتِقَادِهِ رُفِعْ]{.hemistich}[۞]{.verse-sep}[وَكُلُّ مَنْ لَمْ يَعْتَقِدْ لَمْ يَنْتَفِعْ]{.hemistich}
:::

[*Idhi l-fatā ḥasba-ʿtiqādihī rufiʿ, wa-kullu man lam yaʿtaqid lam yantafiʿ.*]{.philo-translit}

[“A learner rises in proportion to his conviction; whoever does not believe in what he learns will not benefit from it.”]{.philo-translation}

[— al-ʿImrīṭī, *Naẓm al-ʿImrīṭī*]{.philo-source}
:::

This line from a classic poem on Arabic grammar is the heart of how I teach: students rise to the level of their conviction. My job is to help them believe that what they learn matters, and that they are able to master it.

::: {.philo-points}
[<i class="bi bi-lightbulb"></i><strong>Why before how</strong><span>Every topic starts from a real problem in networks, data, or systems, so students see why it is worth learning.</span>]{.benefit}
[<i class="bi bi-tools"></i><strong>Learn by building</strong><span>Labs and small projects come before memorisation; understanding grows from making things work.</span>]{.benefit}
[<i class="bi bi-graph-up-arrow"></i><strong>Confidence step by step</strong><span>Small wins, clear feedback, and room to ask questions turn "I can't" into "I can".</span>]{.benefit}
:::
